summary: Victoria Melnikova (Evil Martians) delivers a talk on go-to-market tactics for developer tools, arguing that the founder's personal brand is the most underrated competitive advantage in 2026. She frames the problem: building software is easier than ever, so the bottleneck has shifted to distribution. AI has flooded inboxes and feeds with generated slop, making authentic signal hard to cut through. She introduces the Product Market Fit Compass, a mathematical framework derived from analyzing 37 successful devtools. It plots product signal against revenue: if signal exceeds revenue, distribution needs work; if revenue exceeds signal, product needs work; if balanced, push forward. She notes that 9 out of 10 early-stage devtool startups show product signal stronger than revenue, because technical founders hate marketing. She then lays out six GTM hygiene steps: crystallize value proposition with paying customers, understand developer shelf space, identify distribution channels, become the authority on the problem, map the ecosystem (friends and foes), and distribute early—even before product is ready. Drawing on founder interviews, she prescribes concrete tactics. First, come to San Francisco: David Cramer (Sentry) calls SF 'unfair' for its network effects, and data suggests post-YC startups staying in SF raise twice as much, twice as fast. Second, get loud: Typesense used billboards as a credibility proxy since they lacked funding milestones to publicize. Third, do events—small format meetups, dinners, or full user conferences like Supabase Select. Fourth, do crazy things and embrace failure stories as brand-building opportunities, citing a founder who walked away from $300K ARR to start over. Finally, be unapologetically authentic: Zeno Rocha advises being organic rather than overthinking personal brand strategy. Victoria closes that AI cannot replace a founder's unique personal brand but can amplify it, making founder-led sales and authentic craft the durable moat.

sections.title: Opening: Sam Lambert on Twitter as Customer Acquisition
sections.summary: Victoria recounts a conversation with PlanetScale CEO Sam Lambert at a San Francisco office event. Lambert says Twitter is his favorite thing and that a surprising number of customers come from his personal account. When asked if he tires of it, he insists he'd never give it up. Victoria frames this as the most underrated competitive advantage in 2026: it's not your model, team, or funding—it's you.

sections.title: Context: Evil Martians and the Distribution Bottleneck
sections.summary: Victoria introduces herself as running new business at Evil Martians, a devtool consultancy with a blog reaching half a million technical readers and a podcast called Dev Propulsion Labs. She states that building software has never been easier, so the bottleneck has moved to distribution, and AI has made inboxes and feeds unfilterable with generated slop.

sections.title: Product Market Fit Compass Framework
sections.summary: Victoria presents the Product Market Fit Compass, a mathematical formula derived from analyzing 37 successful devtools. It uses two axes—product signal and revenue. If signal exceeds revenue, work on distribution; if revenue exceeds signal, work on product; if balanced, push forward. She notes 9 out of 10 early-stage devtool startups show signal stronger than revenue because technical founders hate marketing.

sections.title: Six GTM Hygiene Steps
sections.summary: Victoria outlines six foundational GTM steps: crystallize value proposition validated by paying customers, understand developer shelf space, identify distribution channels, become the authority on the problem, map the ecosystem (friends and foes), and distribute early, sometimes before the product is ready.

sections.title: Come to San Francisco
sections.summary: Victoria argues founders should come to SF to meet clients and friends in person. She cites the claim that post-YC startups staying in SF fundraise twice as much, twice as fast. David Cramer (Sentry) calls SF 'unfair' for its network effects, especially for founding and venture pursuits, and urges founders to ignore internet memes and just go.

sections.title: Get Loud: Banners and Billboards
sections.summary: Victoria describes SF's banner culture on Muni buses, buildings, and highways. Banners serve signaling (telling the world you exist, potentially inventing a new category) and earn subconscious mind share. She quotes a Typesense founder explaining that billboards served as a credibility proxy since they lacked funding milestones to publicize; feedback showed people assumed they were big enough to afford hundreds of billboards.

sections.title: Events: From Dinners to User Conferences
sections.summary: Victoria covers event strategy: organizing or attending, small or large. Small formats include paddle, poker, breakfasts, dinners, boba time, technical meetups, and launch parties. She notes the trend of earlier-stage startups hosting user conferences, citing Supabase Select (second year). A founder discusses moving from a no-conference policy to building consensus momentum for hosting one.

sections.title: Crazy Marketing and Embracing Failure
sections.summary: Victoria encourages crazy marketing tactics—flying banners over subs, opening cafes, branding coffee, naming ice cream. She highlights that having fun shows through in marketing. She reframes failure as an opportunity: people love a good fail story, especially with an elegant recovery. A conversation is quoted where a founder walked away from $300K ARR to start from scratch and felt great about it.

sections.title: Be Unapologetically You: Personal Brand as Moat
sections.summary: Victoria closes by urging founders to identify their unique quirks as genius zones and pillars for personal brand. She notes a pendulum swing toward artisanal craft—people love beautiful designs and text despite AI automation. AI cannot replace you but can amplify your signal. Founder-led sales builds trust because people want a real human behind the product. Zeno Rocha advises being organic rather than overthinking personal brand strategy. Victoria calls personal brand the moat that AI will struggle to replace.

demonstrations: Evil Martians' Product Market Fit Compass: a mathematical framework plotting product signal against revenue, derived from analyzing 37 successful devtools to diagnose whether a startup needs to fix distribution or product
limitations: Product Market Fit Compass analysis is based on 37 devtools, a limited sample
GTM tactics are heavily oriented toward San Francisco-based or SF-relocatable startups
Billboard and event strategies require significant budget that early-stage or bootstrapped startups may lack
No specific metrics provided for how many customers personal brand/Twitter actually generates beyond Sam Lambert's qualitative claim
